Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette: Carlos, a 54-year-old Latin American male and business owner, has been struggling with his mental health following his time as a relief worker in a war-torn region. His experiences have left deep scars that have slowly eroded his sense of safety and well-being over the past year. The traumatic event occurred during one of Carlos's missions to deliver supplies to civilians affected by ongoing conflict. Amidst the chaos, gunfire erupted near his vehicle, causing him to crash into a nearby ditch. The sound of bullets whizzing past his head and the sight of civilians running in terror were seared into his memory. Since then, any positive emotion, like hearing celebratory music or laughter, triggers an overwhelming sense of confusion and distress for Carlos. He finds himself jolted back to that moment, struggling to reconcile the joy he's supposed to feel with the fear he can't shake off. Over time, Carlos has developed a series of maladaptive strategies to cope with his symptoms. One of these is rumination; he often goes over and over why the event happened to him, seeking some sense of meaning or control in an otherwise incomprehensible situation. This constant replaying of events in his mind leaves him feeling exhausted and drained, as if he's reliving that moment every day. Another coping mechanism Carlos has adopted is carrying a weapon with him at all times. He carries it not just when he travels to high-risk areas but even while conducting business in the United States. This behavior is driven by a deep-seated belief that he must be prepared for any threat, no matter how unlikely or improbable it may seem. Carlos also finds himself engaging in conflict more frequently. He picks arguments with his staff and customers, often creating drama to distract himself from the trauma he carries. These conflicts have strained his relationships at work, leading to a decline in business performance and an increase in stress levels. His wife has noticed this shift as well, feeling increasingly isolated by her husband's volatile mood swings and constant preoccupation with danger. The combination of these symptoms has created a pervasive sense of unease for Carlos. The gunshot noise that once shattered his tranquility now seems to be lurking around every corner. Even the simple act of walking through crowded streets or being in physical proximity to others can trigger intense anxiety, leaving him feeling like he's constantly on edge. What frightens Carlos most is the fear of never truly finding peace again. He worries that these triggers and avoidance behaviors will continue to dominate his life, preventing him from fully engaging with his family and business. His wife has been urging him to seek help for months, noticing how his behavior has deteriorated over time. Finally, driven by her encouragement and a growing sense of desperation, Carlos decided it was time to reach out. Carlos is most hopeful that therapy can provide some relief and guidance on managing these overwhelming feelings. He hopes to regain control over his life, rebuild the relationships he's strained, and find ways to cope with his trauma without relying on harmful strategies. With this in mind, he has taken a significant step towards seeking help, knowing that recovery is possible if he commits to it. Through therapy, Carlos aims to understand why certain triggers are so potent for him, and how he can navigate them without resorting to destructive behaviors. He hopes to regain a sense of safety and balance in his life, one small step at a time.
